questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a business glossary term and a data dictionary entry, per the lesson's strong answer?
options: A glossary term covers business meaning and can span many tables; a dictionary entry covers one column's technical structure
They are exactly the same thing with two different names
A dictionary is always longer than a glossary term
A glossary only applies to numeric fields
questions.explain: The lesson's strong answer explains that the glossary captures business meaning (potentially spanning many tables) while the dictionary captures per-column technical structure.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should you identify critical data elements for a new regulatory report?
options: Start from what the report discloses, trace every field through its lineage, and flag anything whose error would misstate a regulated number
Mark every field in the source database as critical by default
Only ask the database administrator for their personal opinion
Ignore lineage entirely and guess based on column names
questions.explain: The lesson's strong answer explicitly starts from what the report discloses and traces lineage to find fields whose error would misstate a regulated number.

questions.q: What process does the lesson say should happen BEFORE changing an upstream data object, to avoid breaking downstream dashboards?
options: Impact analysis — walking downstream through documented lineage to find every dependency and notify its owner
Immediately making the change and waiting to see what breaks
Deleting all downstream dashboards preemptively
Root cause analysis, which the lesson says is the same process
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes this as impact analysis (walking downstream before a change), the mirror image of root-cause analysis (walking upstream after a symptom).

questions.q: Per the lesson, when is column-level lineage worth its extra cost over table-level lineage?
options: When a single table has many columns transformed differently and you need to trace one specific number's formula
Column-level lineage is never worth the extra cost under any circumstance
Only when the table has fewer than five columns
Table-level and column-level lineage always cost exactly the same to maintain
questions.explain: The lesson explains column-level lineage is necessary for wide tables with differently-transformed columns, when you need to trace one number's exact formula.

questions.q: How does the lesson say metadata/lineage interview questions typically differ from the open scenario questions covered in Lesson 25?
options: They are often more direct — 'explain the difference between X and Y' or 'walk me through this artifact' — rather than open-ended role-play
They never come up in real interviews
They are always multiple-choice questions on paper
They are identical in every way to scenario questions
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts these more direct 'explain the concept' or 'walk me through' questions with Lesson 25's open-ended scenarios.
